title: Prediction markets tied to clinical trials and drug approvals draw lawmakers' ire
description: The logo for the Food and Drug Administration is seen ahead of a news conference at the Health and Human Services headquarters in Washington, April 22
body: The logo for the Food and Drug Administration is seen ahead of a news conference at the Health and Human Services headquarters in Washington, April 22, 2025.Nathan Posner | Anadolu | Getty ImagesPrediction market event contracts on both clinical drug trials and Food and Drug Administration regulatory approvals are drawing attention from two Democratic senators, according to a letter obtained first by CNBC. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md., and Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., expressed concern over the related event contracts in a Wednesday letter to Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The senators asked what measures HHS has taken to mitigate any risks that may arise from the markets. "Allowing individuals to bet on the success of these trials and drugs undermines the scientific process, creates perverse incentives for researchers, harms trial participants, and could lead to dangerous medical outcomes for untold numbers of Americans," the senators wrote. Alsobrooks and Wyden repeated concerns raised by some healthcare professionals that the markets could alter patient thinking when considering whether to participate in a trial and expressed concern over potential insider trading risks from researchers and regulators who may have access to nonpublic information.Communication requestThe senators requested HHS provide all internal communication regarding staff participation in prediction markets tied to matters governed by the department. They also requested all communication between the department and the prediction market platforms themselves, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission — which regulates event contracts — and any internal analyses that have been done regarding the potential impact of the markets. "HHS, FDA, and [the National Institutes of Health] must uphold the integrity of the drug development process and maintain public trust in the public health by putting essential guardrails in place to prevent individuals profiting on the success and approval of drugs that the American people depend on," Alsobrooks and Wyden said in the letter. Both leading prediction market platforms, Kalshi and Polymarket, offer the contracts, although in Polymarket's case the markets can only be found on its international exchange, which isn't regulated in the U.S.When Kalshi launched its related markets in July, the company said it put in place the guardrails, such as  only allowing markets related to late-stage trials, in order to limit the risk of trading. Kalshi also vowed to list contracts only after a trial had completed enrollment and to use employee verification technology for all traders participating in the markets. "Drug development is one of the most important and most information-constrained industries on earth," Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour said in July. "The data that determines which drugs advance and which don't is largely locked away from the people who need it most. Surfacing information is what Kalshi is for, and we are committed to doing it right."Kalshi, Polymarket and the Department of Health and Human Services didn't immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment.Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

title: Investors pivot to defensive stocks as markets enter a ‘state of alert’
description: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Sept. 16, 2026.Jeenah Moon | ReutersMarkets are in a "state of alert," according to analysts
body: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, Sept. 16, 2026.Jeenah Moon | ReutersMarkets are in a "state of alert," according to analysts monitoring a pivot from riskier tech sector bets into defensive stocks. Technology stocks — a key driver of rallies in recent years — have been notably volatile in 2026. Concerns about artificial intelligence — particularly when it comes to capital expenditure, cash flow, debt and circular financing — have sparked multiple bouts of volatility this year.The Democrats' sweep of Congress in the U.S. midterm elections amplified pressure on the sector last week. Wall Street's tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index is up by around 8.7% since the start of the year as of Nov. 9 close, but gave up some of its year-to-date gains in October when it shed 5.3% over the course of the month. The index — home to Big Tech names including Nvidia, Microsoft, Alphabet and Apple — has staged a recovery in recent days, but remains in the red for November and is down 0.7% for the month so far after dipping into correction territory last week. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNasdaq Composite's performance over the past monthThe Nasdaq isn't the only tech-focused index to have seen big losses over the past month. South Korea's Kospi index, which is heavily exposed to the semiconductor sector, lost 16.2% in October and is down more than 8% month-to-date. The MSCI World Information Technology index lost 7% in October, and has shed a further 4.6% so far this month. MSCI's U.S.-only IT index is down 11.5% since October. At the same time, stocks in defensive sectors have seen broad gains. MSCI's indexes encompassing the consumer staples, healthcare and utilities sectors — widely seen as more stable assets in the equity market during times of volatility or uncertainty — have all risen significantly over the last month. In a note on Monday, Alastair Pinder, HSBC's head emerging markets and global equity strategist, said recent moves in stock markets had been "vicious, and in our view, overdone.""The market is already pricing greater execution risk and capex delays," he said, referring to the development of artificial intelligence. "With US semiconductors trading on a 12-month forward PE of 13.5x after a 45% de-rating since June, how much more pain is there to price?"He added that fundamentals broadly appear healthy. "The rotation into defensives looks extreme," he said. "Walmart trades on 40x forward earnings, near a record high, while Nvidia trades on 13x, near a record low."Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, described equity markets as being "in a state of alert, judging by how investors are rotating their sector exposures.""Such movement matters, and can help stock pickers with their selections, bearing in mind the old adage that 'a bad stock in a good sector will outperform a good stock in a bad sector,'" he said in a note on Monday. AJ Bell's analysis of 11 so-called "super-sectors" in the S&P Global 1200 shows that, in the second half of 2026 so far, healthcare and consumer staples stocks have been the best performers after energy — a major beneficiary of surging oil prices in the wake of the U.S.-Iran war. The IT sector, the data shows, has gone from being the best-performing sector in the first half of the year on a 28.4% rise, to the worst performer in the second half after tumbling more than 11%.  "Information Technology has gone from penthouse to outhouse and slumped from being the best performer to the worst," Mould said. "Energy has been resilient as have Consumer Staples and Healthcare, while Industrials have been noticeably weak. These trends could reflect nagging worries over the economic outlook for next year, as well as worries over whether air is leaking out of an AI 'bubble.'"

schema.headline: Investors pivot to defensive stocks as markets enter a ‘state of alert’

title: American Airlines brings fresh food back to NY-Chicago first class for first time since 2019
description: An American Airlines plane taxis at Chicago O'Hare International Airport in the northwest side of Chicago, Illinois on Jan. 15, 2026.Daniel Slim | AFP
body: An American Airlines plane taxis at Chicago O'Hare International Airport in the northwest side of Chicago, Illinois on Jan. 15, 2026.Daniel Slim | AFP | Getty ImagesAmerican Airlines said Wednesday it's bringing small, fresh "bites" to first class on flights between its hubs in New York and Chicago, the carrier's latest effort to win over higher-spending customers.The changes start this month. Customers will be able to pick between two options, which include prosciutto and melon or apple cinnamon chia pudding for breakfast and a Thai noodle salad or mezze plate for lunch and dinner, American said Wednesday.Read more about airlines' race to win over big spendersAlaska Airlines unveils massive premium cabin overhaul in high-end travel raceBudget airline king Bill Franke warms to first-class seats and premium upgradesUnited ditches more economy seats to make room for bigger premium cabins with new layoutsCaviar and privacy: Airlines' business-class wars are hereAmerican Airlines is arriving late to the luxury travel boom. Can it catch up?First-class seats are getting so fancy they’re holding up new airplanesAirlines can’t add high-end seats fast enough as travelers treat themselves to first classAmerican last offered fresh food for first class on these routes in 2019, a spokeswoman said. Currently, customers in first class on these flights get a smaller, packaged snack. Airlines largely have limited food options for shorter flights, even in first class.American has fallen behind Delta Air Lines and United Airlines in profits and investments in premium options. The airline has been working to step up those premium offerings in recent years with new cabins, lounges and plans for seatback screens on its narrow-body fleets.

schema.headline: American Airlines brings fresh food back to NY-Chicago first class for first time since 2019

title: Tired of spending time fixing other people's AI slop at work? How to talk to them about it
description: You open slides you got from a teammate for a joint project presentation you're giving. Within minutes you suspect that it's largely AI-generated. The
body: You open slides you got from a teammate for a joint project presentation you're giving. Within minutes you suspect that it's largely AI-generated. The stats are incorrect and the writing is littered with generic phrases that sound plausible at a glance but, upon inspection, say nothing of substance. AI was supposed to make work faster and easier, and sometimes it does. Eighty-five percent of surveyed workers, all of whom were active AI users, said the technology saved them between one and seven hours per week, according to a Workday study of 3,200 full-time employees published in January.But as the author of "Managing Up" and an executive coach to high performers at companies like Google, Amazon and JPMorgan, I've seen a new problem emerge. You may regularly find yourself on the receiving end of what looks like finished work that still needs hours of editing. The Workday survey found that nearly 40% of the time "saved" from using AI was then lost to "rework" like verifying, correcting and rewriting.Calling that extra work out to your colleagues and bosses can feel awkward. You might use AI too; 40.5% of employed U.S. adults ages 18 to 64 reported using AI for work in Q3 2026, according to data from the Real-Time Population Survey. So you don't want to sound hypocritical. Plus, you can't always be 100% sure someone used AI, even if it seems obvious to you. So how do you address the extra work landing on your plate without the conversation becoming confrontational? Start with a shared goalBegin by showing that you're not trying to embarrass anyone or prove them wrong. You're on the same side. Frame your feedback in terms of working toward an outcome that preserves the quality of the work and the team's reputation. That way, your intentions are clear, which makes the discussion less adversarial from the outset. Try this:"We both want the executive team to be happy with this.""Since both of our names are on this, I hope you'll agree it needs to hold up to scrutiny from the client." "The goal is for the final version to have the most accurate and up-to-date numbers." Narrow down your concernsAvoid saying, "this whole thing looks AI-generated," especially if you can't prove that. A blanket accusation takes the focus off of what needs to change and puts the other person on the defensive. Instead, point to concrete issues such as vague wording, missing context, hallucinated examples or off-brand visuals. Try this: "A few things jumped out to me that we need to fix before this goes to leadership.""There are two sections where the data could better match what we had previously discussed." "The formatting is different throughout, so I think that needs another quick pass."Mention AI diplomaticallyThis is particularly important when speaking with your boss or someone senior, since you don't want to suggest that you're judging their choices. It can help to acknowledge if you use AI too, which makes it clear that the extra work and the impression the report or presentation could make are the problems, not the tool itself. Try this: "I could be wrong, but some of this reads like AI was involved. I use it too, so that's not the issue. I'm more concerned about making sure we have enough time to edit it before the meeting." "Some of the phrasing and design choices in a couple sections have an AI-generated feel that people are getting more sensitive to. Since I also use ChatGPT and Claude in my work, I'm pretty familiar with some of the 'tells,' and I'd rather remove those so no one makes false assumptions." "People are getting quicker to label certain things AI-generated even when they're not and I'd hate for that to distract from the quality of the work."Set expectations for next timeBe specific about how much time it's already required or will involve to clean up the work and whether it's taken away from other priorities. The other person may not realize the cost unless you explicitly say it. Depending on the relationship, you might ask them to review AI-generated content before sending it over, limit when AI is used or simply flag it up front so you can plan accordingly.Try this: "I've spent time redoing this, which meant pushing back a project for my boss. I hope you understand that's not sustainable. So going forward, can you give AI drafts a quick glance before sending them my way? That'll help me focus my time on core changes.""One thing that would help is knowing when AI was used. That gives me a better sense of how much verification and editing may be needed before it's ready to go so that we don't miss any deadlines." "Because the nuance that comes from your personal experience matters so much for this assignment, what do you think about the initial thinking coming from you? Totally fine if it's messy, and we can always use AI to clean it up later." Remember, your colleagues and leaders are trying to work faster and keep up with ever-growing demands, just like you are. When you push back without shaming them, you show that you respect their intentions while still protecting your time.Melody Wilding, LMSW is an executive coach, human behavior professor and author of "Managing Up: How to Get What You Need from the People in Charge." Get her free training, 5 Steps to Speak Like a Senior Leader, here.

title: Credit card debt climbs to a record $1.29 trillion, New York Fed research finds
description: watch nowAmericans are increasingly turning to credit cards as financial pressures mount, new reports show.Collectively, credit card balances climbed
body: watch nowAmericans are increasingly turning to credit cards as financial pressures mount, new reports show.Collectively, credit card balances climbed by $22 billion in the third quarter to a record $1.29 trillion, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's latest household debt report, released Tuesday. Balances are up 4.2% from a year earlier.Total household debt, including mortgages, auto loans and student loans, also expanded by $334 billion for the July-to-September period to a record $19.1 trillion."Overall debt has been growing," the New York Fed researchers said on a press call Tuesday. "This does reflect financial hardship out there."'One of the most expensive ways to borrow'The average credit card balance per consumer now stands at $6,678, up 2.4% year over year, a separate quarterly credit industry insights report from TransUnion found. The number of people with credit cards rose 2% to 178 million from 174.8 million. Consumers often turn to credit cards in part because they are more accessible than other types of loans — even though the average interest rate on a new credit card offer is about 24%, according to data from LendingTree. Credit card APRs vary depending on the type of card, the issuer and the borrower's creditworthiness. "Credit cards continue to be one of the most expensive ways to borrow," said Charlie Wise, TransUnion's senior vice president of global research and consulting.Andreswd | E+ | Getty ImagesOver time, an increasing share of new credit cards has gone to borrowers with lower incomes and credit scores, and "those accounts are now showing higher levels of distress," the New York Fed researchers said in a corresponding blog post. Credit card issuers loosened their lending standards during the Covid pandemic, and delinquency rates rose in the years that followed, the New York Fed researchers said on the press call."Macroeconomic headwinds — namely high inflation and rising borrowing costs — have squeezed consumers, with inflation outpacing wage growth for low-income brackets," according to the New York Fed.Meanwhile, the cost of living continues to climb, with Americans paying more for essentials such as groceries and gas. Stubborn inflation has now stretched on for years, putting many households in an affordability squeeze. Costs for goods and services rose more than expected again in October, the Bureau of Labor Statistics also reported Tuesday."Higher prices and higher rates have pushed more people into debt," said Ted Rossman, principal consumer finance analyst at Money Management International, a nonprofit credit counseling agency. Balances have continued to swell in the wake of the pandemic, and even though the growth rate is now slowing, "from a household finance standpoint, a lot of damage has been done," Rossman said. The reports come on the heels of the Democrats' strong midterm results, when many voters expressed their dissatisfaction with the U.S. economy, according to Kyle Moore, chief economist at the nonpartisan think tank The Century Foundation. "The throughline connecting so many of Tuesday's outcomes was a recognition that the American economy is failing American families," Moore said, referring to Election Day.Subscribe to CNBC on YouTube.

schema.headline: Credit card debt climbs to a record $1.29 trillion, New York Fed research finds

title: Mississippi Senate: Scott Colom leads Hyde-Smith by more than 3,000 votes
description: Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks with reporters at the OffBeat Records shop in Jackson, Mississippi, Nov. 6, 2026.Brandon Bell | Getty I
body: Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks with reporters at the OffBeat Records shop in Jackson, Mississippi, Nov. 6, 2026.Brandon Bell | Getty ImagesDemocratic nominee Scott Colom extended his lead over incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in the Mississippi Senate election by more than 3,000 votes on Wednesday morning.Colom's lead grew to 3,041 as Hinds County commissioners were set to meet to declare how many ballots had been accepted or rejected in the county. With an estimated 98% of the votes in, Colom led Hyde-Smith 49.11% to 48.79%. Independent candidate Ty Pinkins had 2.1% of the vote.Hinds County, which is the second-most populous county in Mississippi, is a majority Black county that encompasses the state's capital, Jackson. If Colom is elected, he would be the first Black senator from Mississippi since the Reconstruction Era after the Civil War.In 2024, Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris defeated President Donald Trump by 46 percentage points in Hinds County. As of Wednesday morning, Colom was winning 80% of the vote in the county, with just 19% for Hyde-Smith.Mississippi, which has not elected a Democratic senator since the segregationist John Stennis in 1982, was on the radar of few, if any, political analysts as a possible pickup for Democrats. Tuesday was the deadline for resolving affidavit or provisional ballots, which are cast by voters whose eligibility is disputed or unclear on Election Day. It is also the deadline for the receipt of mail-in absentee ballots that are postmarked by Election Day, Nov. 3.Mississippi is one of just two states whose Senate election has not been called. Alaska is the other.Democrats so far have flipped seven Senate seats held by Republicans going into the election. That gives Democrats a new majority in the Senate of at least 54 seats in the 100-member chamber come January.Alaska before Election Day was viewed as possibly key to the question of whether Republicans would retain their narrow majority in the Senate. In Alaska, Democratic nominee Mary Peltola's lead extended to 4,250 votes over incumbent Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan, with 84% of the total votes counted, a margin of 1.8 percentage points. Peltola has 49% of the total vote. If neither she nor Sullivan gets more than 50% of the total vote, the race will go to a ranked-choice round, in which the two other candidates, Gerald Heikes and another candidate named Dan Sullivan, will be eliminated, and the second choices of voters who made them their first choice will be allocated between Peltola and the incumbent.

schema.headline: Mississippi Senate: Scott Colom leads Hyde-Smith by more than 3,000 votes

title: CFTC investigates if Kalshi improperly self-certified event contracts
description: A Kalshi billboard displaying US Congress midterm election odds in New York, US, on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. Angelina Katsanis | Bloomberg | Getty Images
body: A Kalshi billboard displaying US Congress midterm election odds in New York, US, on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. Angelina Katsanis | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Commodity Futures Trading Commission is investigating whether prediction market platform Kalshi failed to properly inform the agency of proposed event contracts, Kalshi confirmed to CNBC.Kalshi called it a minor issue in how the contracts were filed and said it is working with the CFTC to address the matter. The CFTC flagged weather-related contracts, Kalshi said. The leading prediction market platform didn't say when the agency began investigating Kalshi. The CFTC didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.Politico first reported on the probe on Tuesday, noting charges could happen soon, based on the CFTC's private notification to Kalshi. The platform declined to comment on any possible charges. Prediction market platforms are allowed to self-certify event contracts without the federal agency's prior approval, as long as they comply with the Commodity Exchange Act. The self-certification allows for faster  introduction of new contracts. 'Procedural error'"The notice is about a procedural error involving the submission of a handful of contracts, many of which weren't live," said Elisabeth Diana, head of communications at Kalshi. "We are already addressing the issue." The move is the latest by the CFTC as it seeks to rein in prediction markets, which face growing scrutiny in Washington from regulators and members of Congress.In August, the CFTC ordered Kalshi to take down sports-related "mention markets" — where speculators can trade on what individuals will say in a broadcast or speech — while it looked into the event contract type. The agency is also conducting a broad probe into competitor Polymarket, which includes reviewing if the company violated a 2022 settlement with the CFTC to prohibit U.S. traders from accessing its international trading platform. Polymarket's domestic exchange operates separately from the global platform. Prediction markets are also expected to face heightened scrutiny once the Democratic Congress is sworn into office in January. Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., in a Tuesday social media post on X, called for a ban on sports prediction markets — which account for the overwhelming majority of volume on leading platforms. Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

schema.headline: CFTC investigates if Kalshi improperly self-certified event contracts

title: Fed's Goolsbee calls inflation report 'borderline disturbing' as central bank weighs more hikes
description: Austan Goolsbee, President and CEO, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago speaks at The Capital Hilton during the 42nd annual National Association for Busin
body: Austan Goolsbee, President and CEO, Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago speaks at The Capital Hilton during the 42nd annual National Association for Business Economics Economic Policy Conference on February 24, 2026 in Washington, DC. Luke Johnson | Getty ImagesChicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee called the latest inflation data "borderline disturbing." "It's another distressing report — borderline disturbing," Goolsbee said in an interview with "PBS NewsHour" on Tuesday."We've got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing," Goolsbee said. "We're going to have to deal with that."The consumer price index rose 0.4% on a seasonally adjusted basis in October, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Tuesday morning release. That was higher than economists had predicted, and the third straight month of outsized price increases. Goolsbee said he had not seen drivers of prices like tariffs fade over time like he had hoped. He also said continuously high inflation on services concerned him.And the Chicago Fed chief said lofty prices are a top issue for many people he meets."It's on everyone's mind," Goolsbee said. "It's on business mind. It's on nonprofits' minds. It's on ordinary consumers' mind."Tuesday's inflation report landed at a critical juncture for the central bankers at the Federal Reserve as they considers their next interest rate move — and the moves they may have to make in the months ahead if the numbers continue to come in hot.Goolsbee's comments arrived on the heels of remarks from other Fed officials Tuesday who said the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee may need to act more decisively to rein in inflation.When it raises or lowers rates, the Fed typically moves by a quarter-percentage point. But Fed Governor Christopher Waller said in London early Tuesday that a hot inflation report could push him toward advocating for an outsized half-point increase in December, and specifically said such a hike should be on the table if the core CPI, a metric that removes volatile food and energy costs, was "around 0.3." Hours later, that's exactly what happened.Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, speaking Tuesday after the inflation report, said she sees a need for two additional quarter-point increases, and said "it may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the FOMC has moved so far this fall."Anna Paulson, president of the Philadelphia Fed, was more sanguine. While she acknowledged that "inflation pressures are still very much with us," she said Tuesday that the central bank didn't need to move too quickly. "For now, further gradual tightening seems appropriate," she said. "The exact path will depend on how conditions evolve, and I'll be watching the data closely."The committee raised rates by a quarter point in September, to a range of 3.75%-4%, before voting to hold them steady in October.After years of higher-than-preferred price growth, Goolsbee said the possibility of consumers and businesses beginning to expect hot inflation is a "major concern." If that does happen, he said it can make the process of cooling inflation "much more painful."But Goolsbee didn't specify whether he thought the Fed should hike rates at its December policy gathering as a result of these concerns."I'm not a fan of being very specific and tying our hands at the next meeting or meetings in the future," Goolsbee said.Waller, Logan and Paulson are voting members of the FOMC this year, which means they will cast votes on whether to raise rates at the committee's final meeting of the year in December. Goolsbee will be a voting member next year.In the wake of the inflation report and the remarks from the various Fed officials, fed funds futures are now unanimously expecting a rate hike at the December meeting, according to CME's FedWatch tool.Now the question is about whether the central bank will raise rates by a quarter or half percentage point. The fed funds futures currently put the odds of a half-point hike at the upcoming December meeting at 15%. Odds of rates reaching 4.25%-4.5% by the January meeting — the equivalent of either a single half-point rise or two quarter-point hikes — are now at 60%, with a 10% chance of rates hitting 4.5%-4.75% by then.

schema.headline: Fed's Goolsbee calls inflation report 'borderline disturbing' as central bank weighs more hikes

title: American soldier arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia
description: An American flag is displayed on a U.S. Army uniform at Marine Corps Air Station Miramar on September 25, 2026 in San Diego, CA.Kevin Carter | Getty I
body: An American flag is displayed on a U.S. Army uniform at Marine Corps Air Station Miramar on September 25, 2026 in San Diego, CA.Kevin Carter | Getty ImagesA senior soldier in the U.S. Army has been arrested in the U.K. on suspicion of spying for Russia, London's Metropolitan Police said on Tuesday evening. The unnamed 41-year-old man was arrested near Gloucester, a city in western England, on Tuesday as part of an investigation by the U.K.'s Counter Terrorism Policing. British police worked with U.S. authorities, including the military and the FBI, in their investigations.A senior NATO military official confirmed on Tuesday that the American service member was assigned to the military alliance's Allied Rapid Reaction Corps (ARRC). ARRC, headquartered in the English county of Gloucestershire, is a  3-star NATO headquarters with more than 400 permanent staff from more than 20 nations ready to deploy land forces where they are needed. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Wednesday that Moscow had "absolutely nothing to do with" the case in the U.K.The individual at the center of the case, detained in London, is suspected of committing offenses under Sections 1 and 3 of the U.K.'s National Security Act. Section 1 offenses relate to obtaining or disclosing protected information, while Section 3 involves assisting a foreign intelligence service. The maximum penalty is life imprisonment for a Section 1 offense and 14 years' imprisonment for a Section 3 offense. A fine may also be imposed for either offense.Police officers are carrying out searches at two locations in Gloucestershire, the Metropolitan Police added.U.S. mediates Russia-Ukraine talksThe arrest comes as Washington is seeking to broker an end to Russia's war in Ukraine. U.S.-mediated talks between Russian and Ukrainian officials began in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday, the first such meeting since February, while Kyiv and its European allies continue to press for credible security guarantees as part of any settlement.President Donald Trump, a longstanding critic of NATO and its members' defense budgets, said on Monday that there appeared to be a growing willingness on both sides to end the almost five-year war. Russia has long threatened retaliatory action against an expansion of NATO's eastern flank and has previously demanded guarantees that Ukraine will never be allowed to join the alliance. Finland and Sweden became NATO's newest members in 2023 and 2024, respectively. Since Russia and Ukraine have been at war, Russian activity has also been reported deeper into European and NATO territory, with regional authorities investigating whether Moscow could be involved in some of the recent disarray seen across the continent. FBI Director Kash Patel said in a statement on Tuesday evening that the allegations against a U.S. serviceman were "of the utmost concern to the United States and our allies.""I want to send a clear message – this FBI has no tolerance for anyone who breaks their oath to the United States and whose actions endanger our national security and that of our partners," he said. The alleged conduct of a senior solider, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent.Sean StinchonCommanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence CommandSean Stinchon, the commanding general of U.S. Army Counterintelligence Command, said in a statement that "the alleged conduct of a senior solider, entrusted with sensitive information, is a sobering reminder that insider threats are real and persistent."Authorities said Tuesday that the investigation is not related to any other ongoing Counter Terrorism Policing investigations. On Oct. 27, British prosecutors said they had charged a man with assisting a foreign intelligence service over an incident at a military base used by the U.S. for strikes on Iran. The base in question, RAF Fairford, is in Gloucestershire, around 30 miles from ARRC's headquarters at Imjin Barracks.

schema.headline: American soldier arrested on suspicion of spying for Russia

title: Nvidia's Huang tries to project 'business as usual' in return to office after affair revelation
description: watch nowNvidia CEO Jensen Huang walked into the chipmaker's Santa Clara, California, headquarters on Monday and conducted his regular morning meeting
body: watch nowNvidia CEO Jensen Huang walked into the chipmaker's Santa Clara, California, headquarters on Monday and conducted his regular morning meeting with top-level executives, people familiar with the meeting told CNBC.On Sunday, Huang had disclosed an extramarital affair to employees.Huang kicked off the closed-door gathering by addressing his infidelity and sharing how sorry he was to his staff, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly. They said Huang didn't take any questions and quickly pivoted to business and top agenda items of the day.The CEO was also in the office on Tuesday, conducting meetings just one week ahead of the company's quarterly earnings report.Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.Read more CNBC news on NvidiaInside Nvidia: Jensen Huang's first day in office after affair revealNvidia hires law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead Jensen Huang affair probeHuang affair with alleged Chinese spy complicates Nvidia China problemChina panel chair Moolenaar demands answers on Nvidia CEO's alleged affair with a Chinese spyCLUB: Our Nvidia downgrade — plus, Cramer is looking to add to this positionWhat is Megaspeed? The Nvidia chip buyer in the spotlight after Jensen Huang's affairRead Huang's email to his staff and statement from Nvidia's board of directorsNvidia's CEO turmoil gives newly empowered Democrats fresh ammunition in pursuit of oversightPeople inside the artificial intelligence chip giant said Huang tried to project "business as usual," even as the probe moved forward into his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. The CEO was in a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, according to the Financial Times.Sentiment toward Jensen Huang shifted on Sunday after the 63-year-old revealed in an email to employees that he had an affair, though he did not disclose with whom he had the relationship. "I know an apology cannot undo what I have done," he wrote. "I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust." Nvidia's board opened an investigation and hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct the probe on Tuesday.Employees inside the firm described the mood to CNBC as "sad." One employee told CNBC that they were shocked by Jensen Huang's revelations.People also told CNBC that longtime employees viewed Jensen Huang as an idol who could do no wrong and thought of him as a guiding light. Many employees at the company are also struggling to come to grips with the CEO's actions, the people said. Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 to build graphics processing units for video game graphics. In recent years, the company has become synonymous with the AI boom, powering the technology that underpins large language models and the massive data center buildout.A central figure in the development of every AI layer, the Nvidia CEO is also a key voice in Washington, even accompanying President Donald Trump on his trip to China in May. In September, Jensen Huang and his wife were pictured at the same table as Chinese President Xi Jinping for the White House's state dinner.The news of the CEO's affair has drawn increased scrutiny on his continued support for more AI chip sales to China.

schema.headline: Nvidia's Huang tries to project 'business as usual' in return to office after affair revelation

title: Bessent moved to military base amid 'growing threats' from Iran
description: U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent speaks during a press conference in St. Cloud, Minn. on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Leila Navidi | Star Tribun
body: U.S. Secretary of the Treasury Scott Bessent speaks during a press conference in St. Cloud, Minn. on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. Leila Navidi | Star Tribune | Getty ImagesU.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has moved from his Washington home to a military base for his safety amid growing Iranian threats against him.Bessent's move, first reported by The New York Times and confirmed to CNBC by a person familiar with the situation, came as the U.S. war against Iran remains locked in an uneasy stalemate punctuated by intermittent fighting.Concerns about Bessent's security were heightened after The Wall Street Journal "published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located," the person told CNBC on condition of anonymity to discuss the nonpublicized move.The Journal published an aerial view of Bessent's $12.5 million Georgetown mansion in late January 2025, shortly after he bought it.Those security concerns have forced Bessent "to relocate to a military base for his safety," the person said, admonishing the news media to "act responsibly amid growing threats against public officials."Wall Street Journal publisher Dow Jones did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment on the person's statement.The Times reported that U.S. officials have recently seen Iran's plots against American targets reach a more advanced stage and that Bessent's leading role in the ongoing U.S.-Iran war has made him a top target.Bessent has led Operation Economic Outcast, a Treasury campaign launched in August to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and other financial measures, in addition to the U.S. military actions.A Treasury Department spokesperson told CNBC that Bessent "will not be deterred by the Iranian regime's threats."The Cabinet secretary "remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran's economy," the spokesperson added.Bessent's move comes as the Department of Justice said late Tuesday that three Iranian nationals had been indicted on terrorism-related charges. The department said the three were allegedly involved in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the United States.The alleged plots included an attack in September targeting the British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, England, where U.S. military personnel were stationed."Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American service members will be prosecuted by the United States government," Attorney General Todd Blanche said.Earlier in October, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Iran was involved in the incident at RAF Fairford that led to the arrest of five men on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses.Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi then rejected the allegation, writing on X that Burnham was "barking up the wrong tree."RAF Fairford, in Gloucestershire, is a key U.S. Air Force operating location in Europe and has supported deployments of American strategic bombers and other aircraft.The Journal reported Monday that the U.S. evacuated its aircraft from another RAF base in England following a threat from Iran.Stalled negotiations Separately, Secretary of State Marco Rubio reportedly said military action against Iran may not be necessary if economic sanctions and Washington's naval blockade are working.On Monday, President Donald Trump said on Truth Social that "Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, and others, would prefer the status quo, in other words, a continuation of the Greatest Naval Blockade in History.""We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict," Trump added.Asked Tuesday why he would not simply declare an end to the Iran war, Trump said he wanted to ensure that U.S. allies in the region were "not hurt" and that there was a "long-term solution.However, Iranian officials have denied that negotiations are underway. Security chief Mohsen Rezaei said claims that talks were continuing were aimed at "easing economic pressures and reducing oil prices."Brent and West Texas Intermediate crude prices edged higher during Wednesday's Asia trading session, at about $92 and $86 per barrel, respectively.

schema.headline: Bessent moved to military base amid 'growing threats' from Iran

title: Rep. Jim Jordan, Sen. John Thune elected GOP leaders in Congress
description: US Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) speaks to the media on the day of Senate Republican caucus leadership elections at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, Nov
body: US Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH) speaks to the media on the day of Senate Republican caucus leadership elections at the US Capitol in Washington, DC, US, November 10, 2026. Annabelle Gordon | ReutersRepublican lawmakers on Tuesday picked Rep. Jim Jordan of Ohio and Sen. John Thune of South Dakota to serve as their respective House and Senate minority leaders in the next Congress.Jordan, the House Judiciary Committee chairman, was elected in a 106-73 vote, sources told MS NOW on condition of anonymity to discuss the private meeting. He beat Rep. Steve Scalise, R-La., the current House majority leader.A two-decade House veteran and committed supporter of President Donald Trump, Jordan will take on the leadership role just as Republicans relinquish power, following blowout Democratic victories in last week's midterm election.House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced the day after Election Day that he would not run for minority leader in the 120th Congress.Thune, in a statement, said he "appreciated the opportunity to have an open, honest, and transparent conversation with my colleagues today, and I am honored to have their continued trust and support to lead the Senate Republican Conference in the 120th Congress."Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., arrives for the Senate Republican leadership elections in the U.S. Capitol on Tuesday, November 10, 2026. Tom Williams | Cq-roll Call, Inc. | Getty Images"I'm proud of what this Republican team has accomplished together, and we remain united in our commitment to advancing conservative priorities, working with President Trump and our colleagues in the House, and holding the line against Democrats' efforts to enact their far-left, liberal agenda," Thune said in the statement."We have important work ahead of us, and I look forward to serving alongside my colleagues on behalf of the American people," he said.

schema.headline: Rep. Jim Jordan, Sen. John Thune elected GOP leaders in Congress

title: Nvidia shares rebound as Jensen Huang faces scrutiny ahead of earnings
description: watch nowNvidia's stock rose close to 5% on Wednesday, after falling for two days amid the scandal that has rocked the world's most valuable tech comp
body: watch nowNvidia's stock rose close to 5% on Wednesday, after falling for two days amid the scandal that has rocked the world's most valuable tech company.Shares closed down 5.47% on Tuesday as more details were revealed about the impact of CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy. They fell 4.3% Monday.On Tuesday, Nvidia announced it had hired law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate whether company secrets or national security were compromised.Huang tried to project "business as usual" as he returned to the office on Monday, people familiar with the matter told CNBC. The CEO was also in the office on Tuesday, conducting meetings, ahead of the company's quarterly earnings on Nov. 17.Investors are assessing whether the matter will have damaging spillover effects on the business.Stock Chart IconStock chart iconNvidia shares over the past five days.In a Tuesday note, Bank of America said it saw three scenarios with differing investment outcomes. In one scenario, the impact is contained with leadership continuity, and in another, prolonged uncertainty pressures valuation before earnings. In the final scenario, the impact is escalated, with "adverse findings, leadership disruption or tighter restrictions requiring earnings reassessment," BofA research analyst Vivek Arya said in the note.Zacks' Chief Equity Strategist John Blank said the selloff reflected two concerns: that the U.S. might impose further restrictions in the wake of the affair and that further problems might arise as the news develops. "What else has Jensen done?" he said."It's not good for Nvidia. It's not good for Jensen Huang. It's certainly not good for the AI trade," Blank told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday.Morgan Stanley on Wednesday removed Nvidia as a top pick after shares dropped more than 25% since it was named on the list on Oct. 2. Huang's leadership is "crucial" to the company's strategic direction, analysts said in a Wednesday note.— CNBC's Michael Bloom and Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.Read more CNBC news on NvidiaInside Nvidia: Jensen Huang's first day in office after affair revealNvidia hires law firm Wachtell Lipton to lead Jensen Huang affair probeHuang affair with alleged Chinese spy complicates Nvidia China problemChina panel chair Moolenaar demands answers on Nvidia CEO's alleged affair with a Chinese spyCLUB: Our Nvidia downgrade — plus, Cramer is looking to add to this positionWhat is Megaspeed? title: Homeowners tap equity as HELOC balances post biggest jump since 2005: New York Fed report
description: Hispanolistic | E+ | Getty ImagesHomeowners tapped their home equity lines of credit in the third quarter at the highest rate in more than two decades
body: Hispanolistic | E+ | Getty ImagesHomeowners tapped their home equity lines of credit in the third quarter at the highest rate in more than two decades, according to a new Federal Reserve Bank of New York report on household debt released Tuesday. Balances on HELOCs jumped by $23 billion during the three months ending Sept. 30, the largest increase since 2005. That brings the outstanding amount owed to $481 billion, the report shows. This also marks the 18th consecutive quarterly increase. HELOC balances peaked at roughly $714 billion in the first quarter of 2009, according to a 2015 New York Fed report. The current rise in balances comes amid a sluggish housing market, due at least partly to the so-called mortgage rate lock-in effect. Just under half of outstanding mortgages — 49.1% — carried rates of 4% or lower in the second quarter, according to a Realtor.com analysis of federal mortgage data, leaving many owners reluctant to give up their low rates to purchase another home at current higher borrowing costs. The median price of an existing home was $417,500 in September, according to the National Association of Realtors, a real estate trade group. While up just 1.3% from a year earlier, the amount is nearly 54% higher than in September 2019, according to NAR. The average rate on a typical 30-year fixed-rate mortgage is 7.3% as of Tuesday, according to Mortgage News Daily."HELOCs let them borrow against their equity without giving up the low interest rate on their home," said certified financial planner Douglas Boneparth, president and founder of Bone Fide Wealth in New York City and a member of CNBC's Financial Advisor Council.Mortgage holders have $17.5 trillion in equityMortgage holders collectively had $17.5 trillion in home equity as of the third quarter, according to a new report from Intercontinental Exchange, or ICE, a financial markets technology and data company.Tappable equity that can be accessed — meaning a homeowner's equity would remain at or above 20% of the home's value after tapping it — rose 1.2%, or $16,600, from a year ago to an average of $204,000 per borrower, the ICE report shows."Homeowners are sitting on substantial housing wealth, with 2.4 million mortgage holders now holding at least $1 million in equity," Andy Walden, head of mortgage and Housing Market Research at ICE, said in the report. Average HELOC rate is 7.49%HELOCs let you tap a line of credit over time as you need the money, instead of getting it all at once like a home equity loan or cash-out refinance.While HELOCs may have fewer up-front costs than a home equity loan, they generally have a variable interest rate. This means it will move up and down based on a benchmark like the prime rate, which banks use as a basis to set rates on a variety of loans. And, while the Federal Reserve doesn't control that rate, it is influenced by changes the Fed makes to the so-called federal funds rate."If your budget only works at today's rate, then your budget doesn't really work," Boneparth said of HELOCs. "You kind of have to be mindful of the fact that rates may go up."If your budget only works at today's rate, then your budget doesn't really work.Douglas BoneparthPresident and founder of Bone Fide WealthThe average interest rate for a $30,000 HELOC was 7.49% as of Nov. 4, according to Bankrate.Many HELOCs also have a "draw" period when you can take money out, which often lasts five or 10 years. During that time, you typically are only required to pay the interest on any funds you've withdrawn. After that, however, you'll enter a repayment period of, say, 10 or 20 years, when you're required to pay both interest and principal. Because of that, your payments will jump if you've only been paying interest."The real test comes when the repayment period kicks in, and the principal starts to show up, if that's how their HELOC is structured," Boneparth said. "Payments potentially could double overnight, and you really want to know that before you sign anything."watch nowAdditionally, consider what you're planning to use the money for, Boneparth said."If you're borrowing against your home to improve your home, that could make a lot of sense," Boneparth said. "Borrowing against your house to pay off credit cards is a little trickier because you're turning unsecured debt into debt secured by the roof over your head."In that case, if your spending habits don't change, he said, "you're just moving the problem somewhere a little scarier."

schema.headline: Homeowners tap equity as HELOC balances post biggest jump since 2005: New York Fed report

title: CoreWeave CEO Intrator tells CNBC he has canceled his planned share sale program
description: Michael Intrator, co-founder and chief executive officer of CoreWeave Inc., at the Bloomberg Tech summit in London, UK, on Tuesday, Oct. 21, 2025.Chri
body: Michael Intrator, co-founder and chief executive officer of CoreWeave Inc., at the Bloomberg Tech summit in London, UK, on Tuesday, Oct. 21, 2025.Chris J. Ratcliffe | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesCoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC on Wednesday that he has canceled his 10b5 stock sale plan after the company reported strong revenue growth and beat Q3 expectations."Until there is a material change in in, in our equity pricing, my 10b5 has been sidelined," he told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street."He said any further selling would be "just normal tax stuff."Under Intrator's 10b5-1 plan announced in November 2025, the CEO has sold 8.26 million shares at an average price of $96.14 per share for a total of $794.2 million.Intrator and his co-founders have faced criticism for their stock sales as the company's stock has struggled, with shares down 18% so far in 2026 despite a 20% post-earnings rally on Wednesday.The company has faced further pressure from the sell-off in the aftermath of last week's sweeping electoral victory for Democrats, but Intrator told investors on the earnings call that the company isn't worried about the political changes on the horizon."We do not anticipate any impact from the seismic regulatory shift that's occurred," Intrator said on his company's earnings call late Tuesday, in response to a question about new pressures after the election. "We believe that what has occurred is a statement around how you build. We want to build responsibly."Intrator's comments came after CoreWeave reported 168% year-over-year revenue growth, beating estimates, and lifted its forecast for 2026. The stock rallied in extended trading, as the report offered some relief to investors, who have pushed the shares down about 27% over the past month. Read more CNBC tech newsAnthropic IPO meets AI backlash after midterms show stinging rebuke of data centersNvidia’s CEO turmoil gives newly empowered Democrats fresh ammunition in pursuit of oversightCoreWeave confronts 'doom cycle' narrative as neocloud credit risk overshadows growthAmazon’s Astro home robot has fans but looks destined for the ‘trash heap.’ Why it’s trying againRising interest rates and an unfavorable political environment have fueled concerns that the artificial intelligence boom is poised to cool and that companies like CoreWeave will struggle to raise capital. In the Nov. 3 midterm elections, voters sided in favor of greater restrictions on data centers in 40 out of 41 ballot measures in 10 states, according to Ballotpedia. Democrats won control of both houses of Congress and were victorious in governors' races in critical AI infrastructure states like Texas, Ohio and Georgia. In each state, the winning candidate favors some restrictions on new data centers. J.P. Morgan Asset Management wrote in a report after the election that data center projects from 2028 onward are "most exposed," and "face greater uncertainty around permitting, power availability and financing."But CoreWeave says it's not slowing down. The company said it still anticipates 1.85 gigawatts in active power by the end of 2026, and it's now targeting $37 billion to $39 billion in full-year capital expenditures,  implying 155% growth at the middle of the range. Analysts polled by Visible Alpha were looking for $37.69 billion."We are very comfortable with our pipeline," Intrator said, adding that the message from voters isn't a deterrent because the company is always conscious about "being good neighbors.""We think that that is an opportunity for us to continue to scale our business within the new political reality that exists," Intrator said. —CNBC's Nick Wells contributed to this article.WATCH: Steadfastly bullish on CoreWeavewatch now

schema.headline: CoreWeave CEO Intrator tells CNBC he has canceled his planned share sale program
